title: Mistral Large 4 'Le Chonk' arrives as the top open model outside China with improved coding performance and 63% lower cost-per-task
summary: Mistral releases Large 4 open-weight model with improved coding performance and lower cost
detailed: Mistral has released the downloadable open weights for its trillion-parameter Large 4 model under a custom license , giving enterprises a new option for running and customizing a near-frontier AI model themselves.
That puts it one point above Muse Spark Open at xhigh, making ML4 the highest-scoring model with available weights developed outside China in that evaluation.

sentences: Mistral has released the downloadable open weights for its trillion-parameter Large 4 model under a custom license , giving enterprises a new option for running and customizing a near-frontier AI model themselves.
Independent tests now show that its biggest advances over the preview involve efficiency, lower costs and fewer fabricated answers, alongside a small increase in overall capability.
In its October 29 assessment , the independent evaluation firm Artificial Analysis gives ML4 at its high reasoning setting 26 points on Intelligence Index v5, up from 25 for the preview.
That puts it one point above Muse Spark Open at xhigh, making ML4 the highest-scoring model with available weights developed outside China in that evaluation.
It remains six points behind the open-weight leaders, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and GLM-5.3, both tested at their maximum reasoning settings.
The larger change is economic: Artificial Analysis reports that the updated model costs $2.06 per Intelligence Index task, down from $5.54 for the preview, a 63% reduction.
Its coding-agent assessment ranks ML4 second among current open-weight entries, using roughly half the tokens of the leading GLM-5.3 setup.
Mistral’s launch announcement links the downloadable model on Hugging Face and introduces substantially lower API rates.
The release’s Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License makes the commercial boundary explicit.
It contains no revenue threshold.
Instead, the requirement for a separate commercial agreement depends on whether the user or an affiliate operates a model-as-a-service business, subject to specific exceptions.
For Marjorie Janiewicz, Mistral’s chief revenue officer, the commercial argument extends beyond the scores.

In an in-person interview with VentureBeat earlier this week, she described customers seeking models they can retain, customize around their own information and use without depending entirely on a provider’s continuing permission.
“I don’t want to get disconnected.
I want to own my model,” Janiewicz said, describing that customer demand.
“Second, I want to customize it to ensure that I derive value.

And then third, it’s business continuity.”
The independent results sharpen that proposition: ML4 offers a competitive coding agent and improved efficiency, alongside the control that comes with downloadable weights.
They also put boundaries around Mistral’s leadership claims.
Its narrow lead among open-weight models developed outside China does not make it the strongest open-weight model worldwide, and its scores vary with the software and settings used to run it.
When VentureBeat covered ML4 on October 6 , Mistral offered a preview through its API and planned to publish weights on October 27.
The weights arrived on October 29 after roughly three additional weeks of reinforcement learning and feedback from customers and security partners.
The model’s basic identity remains intact: a very large, sparsely activated system that accepts visual and textual information and generates text.
Artificial Analysis now lists a context capacity of 1 million tokens, and its release assessment specifies 1.05 trillion total parameters and 52 billion active parameters.
The development since the preview is additional training and deployment choice, rather than the unveiling of a separate model family.
Some apparent specification changes also need qualification.
Our original report cited 49 billion active parameters; the new release cites 52 billion.
Mistral’s Hugging Face listing explains that the smaller figure describes activity per token, while the larger total also counts embeddings and output layers.
That difference alone does not show that Mistral expanded the model during the preview period.
The latest materials specify 3,800 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs for training, rather than the approximately 4,000 reported initially.

The public launch adds deployment details: Mistral Studio and its API, OpenRouter, Vibe Code, Microsoft Foundry with private Azure deployment options, and Nvidia-hosted endpoints and an optimized NIM container.
Mistral says the downloaded weights can be served with vLLM or SGLang.
Three reasoning settings introduce another practical choice: low replaces the previous “None” mode, medium targets everyday tasks, and high is the default for the hardest requests.
A development team could reserve deeper reasoning for a difficult debugging task and use a lower setting for routine requests.
Whether that reduces the cost of successfully completing work will depend on the task and how often a cheaper attempt needs correction.
The final release combines lower token consumption with API rates of $0.70 per million input tokens, $0.07 for cached input and $2.10 for output.
Artificial Analysis’s new assessment confirms those rates, which are roughly half the earlier $1.36, $0.14 and $4.18 respectively.

AA now measures the economic result for the released checkpoint, rather than leaving it as a projection from token prices:
Source: Artificial Analysis’s October 29 assessment; ML4’s current model page also reports $2.06.
These figures concern Intelligence Index tasks, not Coding Agent Index tasks.
ML4’s cost falls about 63% versus its preview, bringing it close to Muse Spark Open.
Yet DeepSeek and MiMo achieve higher overall Intelligence Index scores at substantially lower measured task costs.
ML4’s favorable output-token usage does not translate into the lowest bill: token rates, input traffic and caching also affect spending.
These benchmark costs do not measure the expense of self-hosting, customization, operational oversight or human review.
Enterprises still need to compare the cost of work completed to an acceptable standard in their own environments.

The final license grants broad rights to run, copy, modify, further train, distribute, sublicense and sell the model and its derivatives, provided the copyright and permission notices accompany copies or substantial portions.
It is a modified MIT license with an additional commercial restriction, so describing ML4 simply as MIT-licensed would omit a material condition.
Section 2 requires a separate commercial license before commercial use of the model or its derivatives if the licensee or any affiliate operates a "model-as-a-service" business.

The definition covers giving third parties access for inference or post-training, through an API, hosted endpoint or other means, when those users have meaningful control over inputs, parameters or training data.

Two exclusions narrow that definition: end-user products whose model capabilities are solely embedded within specific features or harnesses, and services that merely relay requests to models hosted by others.
Section 3 separately exempts internal use that does not make the model or its derivatives available to third parties, as well as use accessed through Mistral’s official products.
That means an enterprise using ML4 internally does not trigger Section 2’s commercial-license requirement, even if it or an affiliate operates a model-as-a-service business.

An end-user product with model capabilities solely embedded within specific features or harnesses is excluded from the model-as-a-service definition; its operator still needs to consider whether another activity by it or an affiliate triggers Section 2.
An operator offering customers hosted inference or post-training with the specified control faces the separate-license requirement before commercial use, subject to the stated exceptions.
The distinction is business activity and access, rather than company size: the model-specific license sets no revenue cutoff.
The permission to run downloaded weights also does not make hosted services or the infrastructure required for self-hosting free.
Artificial Analysis now independently reports ML4’s position on its Coding Agent Index .

The relevant comparison includes both the model and the agent software that directs its tool calls and coding work:
Source: Artificial Analysis’s October 29 assessment and follow-up posts .
Rankings refer to currently available open-weight entries.
ML4 sits one point behind GLM-5.3 and two above DeepSeek.
Its 8.5 million tokens per task represent about 47% less usage than GLM’s 15.9 million, supporting the efficiency comparison in Mistral’s announcement.
Mistral characterizes the scores as effectively tied; Artificial Analysis ranks ML4 second.
